# Exact affine-radius reduction for each half-integer triangle-chain cap

This is a proved variational reduction for the deficit of ONE original
oblique cap. It is not a proof that all affine-radius deficits are
nonnegative, and is not a solution of arbitrary mixed-integer OC.

## Setting and theorem

Let T=conv(0,e_1,e_2), V=area(T), and let the original integer fibers at
bases -h and h+1 be r_h T for h=0,...,m. Suppose

    r_0=R>0, R>=r_1>=...>=r_m>=0,
    r_(h-1)-r_h <= r_h-r_(h+1)  (1<=h<m).

Put t=R/3 and gamma=4/9. Fix ANY a in [1/2,1] and beta>=0, and the
halfspace through the actual own centroid (0,t,t) given by

    -beta z+a x_1+(1-a)x_2>=t.                              (1)

For s in R and r>=0 let F_r(s) be its triangle cap area divided by V:

    F_r(s)=area(rT intersect {a x_1+(1-a)x_2>=s})/V.

Define the actual normalized OC deficit

    D(r)=sum_(h=0)^m G_h(r_h),
    G_h(r)=F_r(t-beta h)+F_r(t+beta(h+1))-gamma r^2.         (2)

The source has normalized total area 2 sum r_h^2; hence D(r)>=0 is
exactly its desired constant 2/9 for the one cap (1).

**Theorem.** If m>=1, there is a slope s in [0,R/m] such that the
affine radii l_h=R-sh satisfy, separately for EVERY h,

    G_h(l_h)<=G_h(r_h).                                    (3)

Thus D(l)<=D(r). The radius replacement keeps the same central fiber,
actual center, normal, integer tilt, integer bases, and number of pairs.
It remains a convex-compatible paired chain. Its total mass need not
be preserved. Every violating original chain therefore yields a
violating affine-radius chain for the very same cap. When m=0 there is
no radius to replace and the assertion is immediate.

## Lemma 1: exact scalar minimizers of every paired deficit

Set

    d_a=a-gamma(2a-1)=(a+4)/9,
    L=2t+beta,
    C=L/(a+d_a),
    rho_h=min{(t-beta h)_+/d_a,C}.                          (4)

Then G_h is strictly decreasing on [0,rho_h] and strictly increasing
on [rho_h,infinity), with the usual interpretation if rho_h=0.

Proof. Write u=t-beta h, v=t+beta(h+1). Thus v>=u and u+v=L.
If u<=0, the left cap is the full r^2 and

    G_h(r)=(1-gamma)r^2+F_r(v),

which is strictly increasing for r>=0. Here rho_h=0 as required.
Assume u>0. For 1/2<a<1 the exact tail as a function of radius is

    F_r(u)=0                              if r<=u/a,
    (ar-u)^2/[a(2a-1)]                    if u/a<=r<=u/(1-a),
    r^2-u^2/[a(1-a)]                      if r>=u/(1-a).

It is continuously differentiable at both knots. For r<u/a the two
caps vanish and G_h(r)=-gamma r^2 is strictly decreasing. Once the
left cap is nonempty, the quadratic coefficient of G_h is at least
1-gamma>0 on every smooth piece: the left cap contributes either
a/(2a-1)>=1 or 1, and the right cap contributes a nonnegative
coefficient. Its first derivative is continuous, so it is strictly
increasing from a negative value and crosses zero once.

If the right cap is still empty, that zero would be at r=u/d_a.
This lies before the left lower-branch knot because

    d_a>=(1-a)  for a>=1/2.

It is the genuine zero exactly if u/d_a<=v/a, equivalently
a u<=d_a v. In that case u/d_a<=C, giving (4).

If a u>=d_a v, both caps have begun by the derivative's zero. If both
are on their upper branches, setting the derivative to zero gives
r=C. The starting-knot condition C>=v/a is exactly a u>=d_a v.
The left finishing-knot condition C<=u/(1-a) follows from v/u<=a/d_a
and

    d_a(2a+d_a-1)-a(1-a)
       =10(2a-1)(5a+2)/81>=0.

Indeed that identity implies
a/d_a <=(2a+d_a-1)/(1-a), which rearranges to the needed condition.
The right finishing knot is no smaller, so C is in both upper
branches. In this case C<=u/d_a, again giving (4). Equality at knots
is harmless since the values and first derivatives match.

At a=1 there is no lower branch: F_r(u)=(r-u)_+^2 for u>0. The same
one-upper and two-upper calculations apply directly with d_a=5/9.
At a=1/2 the tail is (r^2-4u^2)_+ for u>0, so G_h strictly decreases
until r=2u and strictly increases thereafter. Formula (4) gives the
same radius, since d_a=1/2 and C=u+v>=2u. This proves all cases.

## Lemma 2: opposite monotonicity of the two slope sequences

For h=1,...,m define

    p_h=(R-r_h)/h,       q_h=(R-rho_h)/h.                  (5)

Then p_h is nondecreasing and q_h is strictly decreasing, and both
sequences are nonnegative.

Proof. The p_h are averages of the first h nonnegative successive
radius drops. Those drops are nondecreasing by concavity, so the
averages are nondecreasing.

For q_h use the continuous function

    rho(x)=min{(t-beta x)_+/d_a,C},  x>=0.

Its graph consists, in order, of a possibly absent constant segment C,
a possibly absent decreasing affine segment (t-beta x)/d_a, and a
possibly absent zero segment. On each of these intervals the function
q(x)=(R-rho(x))/x, x>0, has derivative respectively

    -(R-C)/x^2,    -(R-t/d_a)/x^2,    -R/x^2.

The middle derivative is negative because t/d_a<=2R/3<R. If the
constant segment is present, then C<=t/d_a<R, so its derivative is
also negative. Values match at every transition. Thus q(x) is
strictly decreasing and positive, including beta=0 (when rho is
constant). Restricting to positive integer x proves the assertion.

## Proof of the theorem

Because p_h is nondecreasing and q_h is decreasing, the set of indices
where p_h<=q_h is an initial segment 1,...,k, with k possibly 0 or m.
Equivalently r_h>=rho_h on that initial segment and r_h<=rho_h on its
complement.

If k=m, choose s=p_m. Then for every h,

    p_h<=s<=q_m<=q_h,

so rho_h<=l_h<=r_h. Lemma 1 gives (3).
If k=0, choose s=q_1. Then for every h,

    q_h<=s<=p_1<=p_h,

so r_h<=l_h<=rho_h. Again Lemma 1 gives (3).
If 0<k<m, choose ANY slope in the nonempty interval

    max{p_k,q_(k+1)} <= s <= min{q_k,p_(k+1)}.              (6)

The interval is nonempty because p_k<=q_k, p_k<=p_(k+1),
q_(k+1)<=q_k, and q_(k+1)<=p_(k+1). For h<=k its choice gives
p_h<=s<=q_h, hence rho_h<=l_h<=r_h. For h>=k+1 it gives
q_h<=s<=p_h, hence r_h<=l_h<=rho_h. Lemma 1 proves (3) in both ranges.

In every case each l_h lies between two nonnegative radii, so l_m>=0.
The selected slope is nonnegative; therefore 0<=s<=R/m. The h=0 radius
has not changed. Finally the affine radii at h>=0, repeated at the
original paired integer bases, form a nonnegative concave full radius
sequence with a flat central pair. The convex hull of these simplex
fibers realizes them exactly, so the replacement is still an actual
mixed-integer source. This proves the theorem.

## Consequence for the previously localized high sector

In the sector a>=2/3, the mass-localized annular theorem proves every
chain whose normalized total mass M is >=9R^2, every beta<=R/78, and
every beta>=R/3. If a violating chain in this sector exists, the affine
replacement is still violating, so it too has M<9R^2. The exact chord
mass bound then forces its number m of outer pairs to satisfy m<=11.
Consequently a high-sector counterexample exists if and only if one
exists among the explicit affine profiles

    r_h=R-sh,  h=0,...,m,
    1<=m<=11,  0<=s<=R/m,
    2/3<=a<=1,  R/78<beta<R/3,
    2R^2<2 sum_(h=0)^m (R-sh)^2<9R^2.                     (7)

No assertion that this remaining three-real-parameter family has
nonnegative deficit is made here. In the lower positive-normal sector
the affine reduction is also valid, but the above mass cutoff has not
been established. All conclusions concern the actual own centroid,
all cap coefficients remain shared by the original fibers, and every
mass in the proof is their exact finite triangle-area sum.
